newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader confident on union, despite clashes.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader confident on union, despite clashes.

text.p: Calm returned to the capital of Belarus on Thursday after clashes over a Union Treaty with Russia, and Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko said he was confident of support for the controversial accord.

"There is a political will on both sides. It is based on wide public support," Interfax news agency said, quoting comments by Lukashenko after he signed the treaty with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Moscow.

Just hours after the accord was signed, in a watered-down version which left the two states clearly sovereign, about 4,000 people marched through Minsk to protest against moves which they fear may eventually rob Belarus of its short independence.
The protest ended in clashes between baton-wielding police and some stone-throwing protesters after about 2,000 of the marchers headed for the Russian embassy.

Witnesses said about 100 people were detained at least briefly and that an unspecified number of people were hurt. Interfax said dozens had been injured but Reuters reporters said the figure seemed lower.
The Union Treaty is intended to deepen integration between the vast Russian Federation of 150 million people and its smaller and less wealthy western neighbour of just 10 million.

But a rearguard action by Russia liberals forced last-minute changes which meant the treaty's practical implications were far less than they would have been under the original draft favoured by Luskashenko who wants a single, unified state.

The liberals said it was too risky to hurtle into uniting two economies at different stages of reform and feared giving the hard-line Lukashenko a foothold in power in Moscow which would raise questions about Russia's democratic credentials.
Lukashenko hit back through his interview with Interfax.
"It is a common victory for common sense," he said of the treaty.

He appeared initially disappointed that the accord had not been reached on the terms he had wanted, but he said he had been encouraged by a meeting with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin after the accord was signed.
"It (the meeting) allowed us to decide many concrete problems on deepening our integration in the first hours of the union's existence," he said, giving no details.

The Russian liberals' opposition, and the protest in Minsk, showed there is resistance to integration. A muted reaction from other former Soviet republics reflected their caution and a wait-and-see approach, if not open concern.

But many ordinary Russians and Belarussians, impoverished by economic reforms, are nostalgic for the Soviet Union which collapsed in 1991. Opposition in Minsk appears limited mainly to students, intellectuals, nationalists and liberals.
"We do not have oil and gas. Russia has it all. We do not need the West and it does not need us. We need Russia and Ukraine, the Slav peoples," said Maria, a 66-year-old pensioner in Minsk.
